methodology: Source-linked original summaries and reference-guided educational reconstructions. Models and motion are unvalidated; artist titles do not independently verify taxonomy. Navigation groups are not a universal kingdom system. Microbial behavior depends on strain and conditions. Expansion entries are individually referenced authored morphology studies; legacy Protista/Monera reporting categories do not replace modern domains. Actual screenshots, software checks and draft status are distinct from independent scientific validation.

Quiet forepaws have a less steep carpal angle with retained supporting digits; sitting keeps the muzzle near level. Jump now has supported compression, distinct airborne limb folding and landing compression without erasing the body lift. This in-place sequence has uncalibrated timing, dimensions and forces. v0.6.4: Authored lateral-sequence walking targets use the same creator skeleton and textured surfaces. Forelimb and hindlimb solvers retain segment lengths; sampled sole support and separate swing clearance replace the generic walking targets. The numerical 70% duty factor, stride and 0.62 Hz playback are illustrative choices, not measured tiger data. Creator Run and all existing same-model postures remain available and unvalidated.

photograph.author: Steven Ward
photograph.description: Decided to drop in at my local spot to see if i could get some Barn Owl action after work as the light was nice.. The owl hunted the banks about 100 metres from me, where I was shooting into the light at the time and eventually after 30 mins worked its way to me and flew past the back of the Auto hide and landed on a post no more than 10 metres away i couldn't believe it!!! Now it had full sun on it (hardly cropped at all). Took 6 shots and he was off. Heart has only just calmed down. It pays to stay in the van. I have been to this spot for a few weeks now waiting to catch him so the waiting game paid off. Wish I didnt have the 1.4x convertor on now to give a bit more breathing space.

photograph.author: Lairich Rig
photograph.description: Cyanobacteria - Nostoc commune. The area in which these colonies were found is the foreground that is shown covered with snow in the following photo: 1158049 . The seaweed-like mass shown here measured 15 cm across. It is a colony of cyanobacteria; specifically, it is Nostoc commune. (For more on cyanobacteria, see 1470400 , taken on the same day, in the same place.) [See http://www.algaebase.org/search/species/detail/?species_id=24479 (at Algaebase) for some pictures, and for detailed taxonomic information.] Within its outer membrane, the colony contains a brownish gel in which chains of green cells are suspended. The colonies vary greatly in appearance according to how wet they are, but are generally olive-green to brown. Although I've shown a single specimen here, the area was covered in seaweed-like patches, up to several square metres in size. Two factors account for the abundance: (1) for the west of Scotland, the summer of 2009 was the second wettest since records began in 1914, and (2) there is great deal of concrete here, from large chunks to tiny fragments (the Nostoc pruniforme link, above, explains why this favours their growth). The abundance of N. commune was not confined to this spot; later on the same day, I noticed that a little concrete footbridge (NS 3984 7708) across the Murroch Burn in Kilmalid was also densely covered. photograph.author: James St. John
photograph.description: Clypeaster rosaceus Lamarck, 1816 - washed ashore onto a rocky shoreline. Irregular echinoids have somewhat globular skeletons (tests) composed of interlocking calcite plates and covered in short, fur-like spines. The skeleton is bilaterally symmetrical, not pentaradially symmetrical as in the sea urchins. The upper side of the skeleton has the pattern of a 5-petaled star - each petal is an ambulacrum. The mouth and anus are at opposite ends of the long axis of the skeleton. Heart urchins are infaunal deposit feeders - they consume bulk sediments, digest any organic matter mixed in, and excrete large quantities of sediments. In the specimen shown above, decay has resulted in the spines being detached - the small pustules are spine attachment bases. Locality: beach landward from Snapshot Reef, Fernandez Bay, western San Salvador Island, eastern Bahamas

photograph.author: Diego Delso
photograph.description: Snakelocks anemone ( Anemonia viridis ), Arrábida Natural Park , Portugal. The snakelocks anemone is a predator , related to jellyfish (but without a medusa stage in their lifecycle), that ensnares prey of suitable size that comes within reach of its tentacles immobilizing it with the aid of their nematocysts (explosive cells that contain one giant secretory organelle that can deliver a sting). The prey is then transported to the mouth and thrust into the pharynx. This species is widely consumed in Andalusia and is known as ortiguillas de mar (literally, "little sea nettles", because it has urticant properties before it is cooked). The whole animal is marinated in vinegar , coated in a tempura-like batter , and deep-fried in olive oil .

photograph.author: Diego Delso
photograph.description: Cylinder anemone ( Cerianthus membranaceus ), Arrábida Natural Park , Portugal. This tube-dwelling anemone has an oral disc with a diameter of up to 40 cm (16 in). There are two whorls of tentacles, amounting to about two hundred tentacles in all. Those in the outer whorl are long and slender and armed with cnidocytes (stinging cells) and are used for catching prey. Tentacles in the inner whorl are shorter and function to transfer captured food to the central mouth. This species is found on the seabed in shallow water in the Mediterranean Sea, the northern Adriatic Sea and the northeastern Atlantic Ocean, its range extending as far north as Britain. The tentacles of Cerianthus membranaceus do not retract, but the whole animal can retreat into its tube. As it does so, some of the tentacles grip the rim and pull the tube closed behind it, effectively making it disappear from view. The tube is normally a permanent home, but if the anemone is disturbed from below, as by a burrowing sea urchin, it can eject itself from its tube, move to a new location and secrete a new tube. C. membranaceus feeds on small fish and planktonic organisms which it catches with its tentacles. It is a protandrous hermaphrodite , starting life as a male and becoming a female later. photograph.author: Content Providers(s): CDC/ Matthew J. Arduino, DRPH Photo Credit: Janice Haney Carr
photograph.description: Under a very high magnification of 20,000x, this scanning electron micrograph (SEM) shows a strain of Staphylococcus aureus bacteria taken from a vancomycin intermediate resistant culture (VISA). Under SEM, one can not tell the difference between bacteria that are susceptible, or multidrug resistant, but with transmission electron microscopy (TEM), VISA isolates exhibit a thickening in the cell wall that may attribute to their reduced susceptibility to vancomycin . See PHIL 11156 for a black and white version of this image. VISA and VRSA are specific types of antimicrobial-resistant staph bacteria. While most staph bacteria are susceptible to the antimicrobial agent vancomycin some have developed resistance. VISA and VRSA cannot be successfully treated with vancomycin because these organisms are no longer susceptibile to vancomycin. However, to date, all VISA and VRSA isolates have been susceptible to other Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved drugs. How do VISA and VRSA get their names? Staph bacteria are classified as VISA or VRSA based on laboratory tests. Laboratories perform tests to determine if staph bacteria are resistant to antimicrobial agents that might be used for treatment of infections. For vancomycin and other antimicrobial agents, laboratories determine how much of the agent it requires to inhibit the growth of the organism in a test tube. The result of the test is usually expressed as a minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) or the minimum amount of antimicrobial agent that inhibits bacterial growth in the test tube. Therefore, staph bacteria are classified as VISA if the MIC for vancomycin is 4-8µg/ml, and classified as VRSA if the vancomycin MIC is >16µg/ml.

photograph.author: Olivier Dugornay (Ifremer)
photograph.description: The crab is found in the North Sea, the English Channel, the North-East Atlantic and the Mediterranean. Its shell measures 5 to 6 cm in length and 8 cm in width. It is brownish in colour, with appendages with blue lines and bright red eyes. There are 4 to 5 teeth on the shell on either side of the eyes. Its hind legs, called "swimming legs", have a characteristic flattened shape. Here we see two individuals in the reproductive phase: the male embraces the female during her moulting period, the only period when she is receptive. This embrace can be long. The reproductive period is between February and November. A pink carpet of anemone corinactis, also called jewel anemone, surrounds the crabs. This anemone is present in the English Channel, the Atlantic and the Mediterranean. Its color is often bright, with slightly translucent tentacles with a more colorful bulge at their end. Most of the individuals photographed here are closed.

photograph.file: Araignée mâle sur fond de maërl (Ifremer 00557-66908 - 20311).jpg
photograph.author: Olivier Dugornay
photograph.description: The Atlantic spider crab ( Maja brachydactyla ) is a crustacean. It is found in the waters of the North Sea to the Canaries, on sandy or rocky bottoms, between the surface and 50 m deep. Here, it is a male individual, photographed in the harbor of Brest on a bottom of maërl (accumulation of coralline algae common in Brittany). Its shell, strongly domed and rounded, can measure up to 25 cm long and 18 cm wide. Its legs, with significant hairiness, are long and thin. Note that, unlike other crustaceans, the spider crab has a terminal moult, which has the consequence of stopping its growth abruptly. Its fishing is subject to regulation: see Berne Convention (relating to the conservation of wildlife and natural habitats in Europe): Annex III – Protected species .
